newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 14.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Monday:
* Despite Friday's steep decline in the stock market, investors appear to be holding relatively steady.

* Singapore shipping firm Neptune Orient Lines said it agreed to buy APL, the leading container carrier in Pacific markets doing 10 percent of the business between North America and East Asia, for $825 million.
* Patriot American is expected to announce plans to buy the Wyndham hotel chain for about $640 million.
* Film production company Destiny Pictures has offered stock in its low-budget film over the Internet.
* Cox Communications customers seem to like their cable company and Wall Street is also paying attention.
* A number of changes to patent law have been proposed under a Congressional bill, including turning the U.S. Patent Office into a semi-private corporation.
* Market place: The Dow Jones industrial average last fell 10 percent from a record high in 1990 and some say the damage to stock portfolios has been more severe than that.
* Publishers wonder if everyday prose, as opposed to unique expression, can really be plagiarised.
* Retail web sites are starting to join with sites devoted to information which have text, pictures or graphics.
* The pace and exact scope of deregulating the U.S. electric power industry is generating much debate in Congress and across the country.
* The lawyer who won a judgment last year against Brown & Williamson Tobacco will be involved in another closely-watched trial involving the cigarette industry this week.
* House Speaker Newt Gingrich said he favoured extending China's normal trading status with the United States for six months instead of the usual year.
* On web sites like A.F.L.-C.I.O.'s Executive Pay Watch you can learn information like how many years you will have to work to earn as much as the chairman makes in an hour.

* News analysis: Broadcasters at this year's National Association of Broadcasters convention in Las Vegas were preoccupied with digital high-definition television and who would reap the profits from gearing up television stations to offer the new programming.
